title: Trump-Era EPA Rescinded Methane Standards for Oil and Gas Production and Processing
description_short: In August 2020, Trump-era EPA removed transmission and storage from oil-and-gas standards and rescinded methane rules for production and processing.
description_medium: On August 13, 2020, EPA issued final amendments to the New Source Performance Standards for the oil and natural gas industry. The policy amendments removed transmission and storage from the standards and rescinded methane requirements for production and processing. EPA described the changes as simplifying the rules and reducing regulatory burdens.
description_long: On August 13, 2020, during Donald Trump’s first administration, EPA issued final policy amendments to the New Source Performance Standards for the oil and natural gas industry. These standards set federal requirements for covered sources in the sector. EPA’s summary says the amendments removed the transmission and storage segment from the standards and rescinded methane requirements for the production and processing segments. The agency described the changes as simplifying the regulatory program and reducing burdens on industry. EPA’s webpage identifies the action as final policy and technical amendments to the standards and a related Congressional Review Act resolution. The stated changes concern the coverage and methane requirements of these oil-and-gas standards. This account does not claim that the rule addressed every source of methane or quantify the change in emissions. The cited EPA summary establishes the date, affected segments and agency-stated rationale, while leaving any measured environmental outcome unspecified.

supports: EPA issued final amendments on August 13, 2020; removed transmission/storage from the standards and rescinded methane standards for production/processing.
EPA characterized the action as policy and technical amendments and described its stated rationale.
limitations: The page does not quantify resulting emissions changes.

rationale: The official EPA summary is accessible and supports the August 2020 action and the affected standards. The previous BBC URL concerns a separate endangerment-finding event, so it is removed; the revised copy attributes the rationale to EPA and makes no quantified emissions claim.
correction_proposal: Replace the unrelated BBC citation with EPA’s 2020 rule page and retain only the specific changes to the oil-and-gas standards.

text.description_short: EPA’s August 2020 rule rescinded methane standards for oil and gas production and processing and removed transmission and storage from the rule.
text.description_medium: On August 13, 2020, EPA issued final policy amendments to oil and gas New Source Performance Standards. The amendments removed the transmission and storage segment from the rule and rescinded methane standards for production and processing segments. The linked BBC article concerns a separate 2026 endangerment-finding action and does not support this event.
text.description_long: On August 13, 2020, the Environmental Protection Agency issued final policy amendments to the New Source Performance Standards for the oil and natural gas industry. EPA said the amendments removed the transmission and storage segment from the standards and rescinded methane emissions requirements for production and processing segments. The agency described the rules as simplifying and reducing burdens on industry; environmental groups criticized the rollback because it weakened federal methane controls. The event concerns specific standards adopted under the Clean Air Act, not the later greenhouse-gas endangerment finding discussed in the linked BBC article. The original BBC URL therefore does not support the event and should be replaced with EPA’s rule page or contemporaneous rulemaking materials. This account identifies the provisions changed without adding an unsupported estimate of emissions effects. EPA’s own summary establishes the date and segments affected, while the policy rationale should be attributed to the agency rather than presented as an independent finding.

title: Trump Order Exempted Listed Federal Agencies from Labor-Relations Statutes
description_short: A March 2025 order exempted specified federal agencies and components from federal labor-management relations programs.
description_medium: President Trump’s March 27, 2025 executive order excluded listed agencies and agency subdivisions from federal labor-management relations statutes, invoking national-security authority. The Office of Personnel Management’s implementation memo identifies covered organizations. The order changed labor-relations coverage for the listed federal units; it did not eliminate unions or collective bargaining across federal, state and private employment.
description_long: President Donald Trump signed Executive Order 14251, titled “Exclusions From Federal Labor-Management Relations Programs,” on March 27, 2025. The order invokes statutory authority to exempt listed federal agencies and subdivisions from the Federal Service and Foreign Service labor-management statutes. An Office of Personnel Management implementation memorandum says covered organizations are no longer required to collectively bargain with federal unions and that unions lose exclusive-recognition status for those covered units. The order changes bargaining rights for named federal components. Its scope is limited to listed federal agencies and subdivisions; it does not eliminate unions or collective bargaining across all public and private employment. The order also authorizes agency heads to identify further qualifying subdivisions under its terms. The Federal Register published the order on April 3, 2025, and OPM guidance describes implementation for covered organizations. These provisions address federal labor relations statutes, not state or private-sector organizing.

supports: Trump signed EO 14251 on March 27, 2025; it lists federal agencies and subdivisions excluded from labor-management statutes.
limitations: Does not establish a universal public- or private-sector ban.

supports: OPM explains implementation for covered organizations, including bargaining and exclusive-recognition status.
limitations: Applies to listed covered federal units.

supports: The published order text, date, statutory basis and covered scope.
limitations: Does not establish the original universal union-elimination claim.

rationale: The proposal corrects the frozen universal union-ban claim to the enacted EO 14251 scope. The White House order, OPM implementation guidance and Federal Register text support the stated date, covered federal units and labor-relations effect; the copy avoids extending the order to state or private employment.
correction_proposal: Replace the frozen universal union-elimination claim with the narrower EO 14251 account and keep Project 2025 material as policy context only.

text.description_long: President Donald Trump signed Executive Order 14251, titled “Exclusions From Federal Labor-Management Relations Programs,” on March 27, 2025. The order invokes statutory authority to exempt listed federal agencies and agency subdivisions from the Federal Service and Foreign Service labor-management statutes. An Office of Personnel Management implementation memorandum states that covered organizations are no longer required to collectively bargain with federal unions and that unions lose exclusive-recognition status for those covered units. The order therefore materially changes bargaining rights for named federal components. Its legal scope is the listed federal agencies and subdivisions; it does not eliminate unions or bargaining across all public and private employment. The executive order also includes mechanisms for agency heads to identify further qualifying subdivisions under its terms. The supplied Project 2025 and labor-group sources provide policy context, but the official order and OPM memo establish what was enacted. This account replaces the original claim of complete union elimination with the documented federal-sector change and keeps the policy’s limited coverage clear.

Donald Trump achieved complete elimination of labor unions by banning collective bargaining for all federal workers while implementing Project 2025's plan to 'end public sector unions' and make private sector organizing illegal through systematic destruction of National Labor Relations Act protections and worker rights that had enabled collective action for over 90 years. The comprehensive union destruction represented Trump's implementation of corporate control over American workers by eliminating every protection for collective bargaining while enabling employers to retaliate against organizers, decertify existing unions mid-contract, and create company-controlled sham unions that served management interests rather than worker welfare. The collective bargaining ban included directing NLRB to prosecute union leaders for political advocacy while allowing employers to negotiate away overtime protections, workplace safety requirements, and fair scheduling in exchange for token benefits that reduced worker power and economic security. Trump's union elimination violated fundamental worker rights by destroying legal protections that had enabled collective action while creating 'union-free' environment where workers faced employer retaliation without legal recourse or organizational support to address workplace abuse, wage theft, and unsafe conditions. The worker rights destruction created what labor advocates called systematic return to 'Gilded Age' exploitation where employers gained complete control over working conditions while eliminating worker voice in workplace decisions, economic security, and safety protections that unions had historically provided through collective bargaining. The complete union elimination represented Project 2025's vision of labor relations controlled by corporate interests rather than worker rights, transforming employment from protected relationship with collective bargaining into 'at-will' system where workers lacked voice, representation, or legal protection against employer abuse and exploitation through systematic elimination of labor organizing and collective action.

title: Trump Removes Rex Tillerson and Nominates Mike Pompeo as Secretary of State
description_short: Trump Removes Rex Tillerson and Nominates Mike Pompeo as Secretary of State
description_medium: On March 13, 2018, Donald Trump announced that Rex Tillerson would leave as Secretary of State and nominated CIA Director Mike Pompeo to succeed him. Pompeo’s nomination required Senate confirmation. The announcement changed department leadership; the available reporting does not establish a corrupt exchange, favoritism or obstruction as its motive.
description_long: On March 13, 2018, President Donald Trump announced that Secretary of State Rex Tillerson would leave the administration and nominated CIA director Mike Pompeo to succeed him. Tillerson had led the State Department since the start of Trump’s first term. Pompeo’s nomination proposed moving him from the CIA to the country’s senior diplomatic post and required Senate confirmation. The announcement changed the leadership of the department responsible for U.S. diplomacy, while the nomination alone did not complete the transition. The available reporting does not establish a corrupt exchange, favoritism or obstruction as the motive. It also does not identify policy consequences that followed from the change. The March 13 announcement records a personnel decision; Pompeo’s later confirmation and tenure as secretary are separate developments. The nomination required Senate confirmation before Pompeo could assume the post. The announcement concerned the executive branch’s foreign-affairs leadership and a proposed move between two senior administration posts.

supports: The supplied event-specific link title identifies Trump’s March 13, 2018 Tillerson departure announcement and Pompeo nomination.
limitations: CNBC returned HTTP 403 in the focused check; the accessible AP link in the prior record was only a general topic hub.
No cited material establishes corruption, favoritism or obstruction.

title: Trump Grants a Full Pardon to Otis Gordon on December 22, 2020
description_short: The archived White House says Trump granted a full pardon to Otis Gordon on Dec. 22, 2020.
description_medium: An archived White House statement dated Dec. 22, 2020 says President Donald Trump granted a full pardon to Otis Gordon. It says Gordon had been convicted of possession with intent to distribute and identifies Sen. Tim Scott as supporting the pardon. The statement does not document bribery, favoritism or a corrupt exchange.
description_long: An archived White House statement dated December 22, 2020 says President Donald Trump granted a full pardon to Otis Gordon, one of 15 people pardoned that day. It says Gordon had been convicted of possession with intent to distribute, later became a pastor at Life Changer’s International Ministries and mentored at-risk youth. The statement identifies Senator Tim Scott as a supporter of the pardon and spells the recipient’s name “Otis Gordon,” without a middle initial. The action described is a full pardon, rather than a commutation. The statement gives no evidence of bribery, a financial benefit to Trump, favoritism or another exchange connected to the grant. The archived announcement describes the pardon and Gordon’s community work; it does not give a reason for the grant or evidence of an exchange. The American Presidency Project page reproduces the same archived White House statement.

limitations: The statement does not establish a corrupt exchange or motive.

title: The Atlantic’s Unthinkable Package Cataloged 50 Trump Presidency Moments
description_short: The Atlantic published a curated list of 50 incidents it said defined the first two years of Trump’s presidency.
description_medium: On Jan. 22, 2019, The Atlantic presented “Unthinkable: The 50 Moments that Define the Trump Presidency,” an editorial project marking the midpoint of Trump’s first term. The package described its 50 selected incidents as improbable, norm-bending and destructive. This supports the existence and scope of the retrospective, not a causal effect on institutions or accountability.
description_long: The Atlantic’s Unthinkable page presents “Donald Trump’s 50 Most Unthinkable Moments,” a curated retrospective of the first two years of his presidency. Its January 22, 2019 event page says the project marked the midpoint of Trump’s first term and selected 50 incidents the editors described as improbable, norm-bending and destructive. The package is an editorial collection about events from Trump’s presidency, with the publication’s own framing of those events. The Atlantic pages describe a retrospective publication. title: Ivanka Trump Testifies in DC Inquiry into Inaugural Committee Spending
description_short: Ivanka Trump Testifies in DC Inquiry into Inaugural Committee Spending
description_medium: On December 1, 2020, Ivanka Trump sat for a deposition with the D.C. attorney general’s office during its investigation into the 2017 Trump Presidential Inaugural Committee. ABC News reported that the inquiry examined committee spending at the Trump International Hotel. Her lawyer said she connected the parties and told the hotel to charge a fair-market rate. The report identifies no knowingly false answer or finding of perjury.
description_long: On December 1, 2020, Ivanka Trump gave a deposition to the Washington, D.C., attorney general’s office during its investigation of the Trump 2017 Presidential Inaugural Committee. ABC News reported that investigators were examining committee spending, including payments for event space at the Trump International Hotel in Washington. The D.C. attorney general’s filing compared a $5,000 charge for a prayer breakfast using the venue earlier on Inauguration Day with the committee’s later $175,000 payment for the same event space. Ivanka Trump’s lawyer told ABC that her role was limited to connecting the parties and instructing the hotel to charge a fair-market rate. These are reported investigative allegations and an attorney’s characterization of her role, not a judicial finding about her conduct. The report confirms the deposition but identifies no knowingly false answer, perjury charge or perjury finding. The report concerns testimony in the civil inquiry and does not establish that Ivanka Trump lied under oath.

description_short: Trump said on August 20, 2025, that his administration would not approve wind or solar projects; the post alone does not define implementation.

title: Trump’s January 2016 Iowa Veterans Fundraiser Sent $2.823 Million to His Foundation
description_short: Trump’s Jan. 28, 2016 Iowa veterans fundraiser raised $5.6 million; $2.823 million went to his Foundation, according to New York Attorney General filings.
description_medium: On January 28, 2016, Donald Trump held an Iowa fundraiser for veterans’ organizations rather than attend a televised Republican debate. New York Attorney General filings say the event raised about $5.6 million and that $2.823 million went to the Trump Foundation. The Attorney General later alleged that the Foundation’s handling of the funds constituted an improper campaign contribution. This fundraiser is separate from the $2 million damages order issued in 2019.
description_long: On January 28, 2016, Donald Trump held a nationally televised fundraiser in Iowa for veterans’ organizations while skipping a televised Republican debate. New York Attorney General filings say the event raised approximately $5.6 million and that $2.823 million was donated to the Trump Foundation, which was expected to distribute the money to veterans’ groups. The Attorney General later alleged that the Foundation ceded control of the grants to Trump’s campaign, making its contribution an improper in-kind campaign contribution. That statement is an allegation, not a finding that every fundraiser dollar was misused. In November 2019, a court separately ordered Trump to pay $2 million in damages to charities and imposed restrictions on future charitable service. The fundraiser took place nearly four years before the November 2019 judgment. The Attorney General’s allegation and the later court-ordered damages are separate legal developments.

title: Trump Fires Inspectors General Across Federal Agencies in January 2025
description_short: Trump fired inspectors general at multiple federal agencies in a late-night January 2025 move.

The contemporaneous report raised questions about statutory advance-notice requirements to Congress without resolving their legality. The January and June episodes are separate rounds of dismissals.

title: Banker Testified Trump’s Financial Statements Supported Doral and Chicago Loans
description_short: A retired bank official testified that Trump financial statements were key to a $125 million Doral loan in 2011 and a $107 million Chicago hotel loan in 2012.
description_medium: At Trump’s October 2023 New York civil-fraud trial, a retired bank official testified that Trump’s financial statements were key to approving a $125 million loan for his Doral golf resort in 2011 and a $107 million loan for his Chicago hotel in 2012. This testimony concerns lending and financial statements; the cited AP report does not establish double-billing through internal loans or a court finding on that mechanism.
description_long: An Associated Press report from October 11, 2023 described testimony by a retired bank official at the New York civil-fraud trial brought by Attorney General Letitia James against Donald Trump, his company and top executives. The official testified that Trump’s financial statements were key to the bank’s approval of a $125 million loan in 2011 for Trump’s Doral golf resort in Florida and a $107 million loan in 2012 for his Chicago hotel and tower. AP reported that this was the first time a bank official testified in court about the statements’ effect on Trump’s ability to obtain loans. The trial concerned whether financial statements used for lending were fraudulent, but this testimony does not establish that expenses were billed twice through internal loans. It also does not amount to a court finding on that alleged mechanism. This testimony concerns loan approvals and does not establish a separate internal-loan expense transaction.
